title: Slot-based KV Quotas and Deferred Batch Eviction for OOM Recovery
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Summary:
We observed multiple incidents where continuous batching combined with aggressive KV cache growth caused GPU resident memory to spike and trigger OOMs during sudden high-concurrency bursts of long-context requests. Existing eviction heuristics are reactive and cause head-of-queue latency spikes and dropped requests. This ticket proposes an admission + accounting layer (slot-based KV quotas) coupled with a deferred batch-eviction path and graceful fallback routing to prevent hard OOMs and provide predictable recovery behavior.

Goals:
- Prevent process-level OOMs by bounding per-request KV residency via slot quotas and soft-eviction windows.
- Ensure graceful degradation: requests hit a deterministic fallback (reduced batch size, quantized model, or short-circuit streaming) rather than abrupt failures.
- Maintain fairness across tenants and preserve SLOs for high-priority routes.
- Provide observability: quota utilization, evicted-kv-rate, admission-reject-rate, and per-tenant latency/cost impact.

Design proposal (high level):
1) Slot-based KV Quotas
   - Each incoming request is assigned a number of "KV slots" proportional to its estimated KV pressure (sequence length, token window, attention sparsity hints). Slots map to a small fixed memory budget unit so accounting is cheap.
   - The admission controller tracks total free slots per GPU and refuses/queues requests when free slots < threshold. Refused requests follow fallback rules.

2) Deferred batch eviction (async compaction)
   - When memory pressure rises, instead of immediate full-eviction (which spikes latency), mark candidates for compaction and perform background async compaction/snapshotting of non-hot KV shards into a compressed store (local NVMe or remote fast object). This reduces resident memory without blocking live batches.
   - Compaction is prioritized by LRU+request-priority and constrained by a compaction-rate limiter to avoid IO storms.

3) Graceful fallback routing
   - Admission controller triggers one of deterministic fallback actions in order of preference per-route: (a) reduce batch admission quota (admit fewer requests into the batch), (b) route to quantized model variant for that tenant, (c) activate short-token streaming mode (truncate generation to safe token window), (d) fall back to a cross-region capacity pool.
   - Fallback preferences are configurable per-customer/route and plumbed through the route config in the control plane.

4) Prefetch / estimation improvements
   - Improve request KV pressure estimation by sampling previous sessions and using a lightweight ML model to predict effective KV size from prompt metadata. This reduces over-allocation and wasted slots.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Spike (1 week): implement slot accounting shim in runtime, add metric hooks. Run synthetic stress tests to validate that slot accounting bounds resident KV. (Spike PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2345)
- Prototype deferred compaction (2 weeks): implement marking + background compactor with NVMe-backed compressed store; expose compaction metrics and a dashboard (Grafana panel: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv-compaction).
- Admission + fallback rules (2 weeks): wire per-route preferences to control plane, implement fallback actions and end-to-end tests.
- Canary rollout (1 week): enable on a small dedicated pool, monitor rejects, latency, and cost delta.

Key metrics to track:
- resident_kv_bytes_per_gpu, free_kv_slots, admission_reject_rate, compaction_rate_bytes/s, fallback_activation_count, per-route p95 latency, OOM_count

Tradeoffs and open questions:
- Latency vs memory: deferred compaction introduces background IO which can compete with inference IO; need to tune compaction-rate limiter.
- Fairness: slot quotas may penalize bursty low-priority tenants. We propose priority buckets and emergency preemption for P0 customers.
- Complexity: compressed NVMe store increases operational surface (disk failures, hotspotting). Consider SLOs for compaction store availability.

Testing and validation:
- Synthetic large-context stress tests across 0.5–2.0M tokens/sec to validate slot exhaustion leads to predictable rejections instead of OOMs.
- End-to-end canary with real traffic on dedicated pool; run chaos tests (kill compactor, saturate NVMe) and verify graceful fallback.
- Automated regression: unit tests for accounting, integration tests for fallback paths, nightly memory-usage baselines.

Rollout strategy:
- Feature flag gated. Start with non-critical tenants and a single GPU pool. Canary for 72 hours, measure OOM_count==0 and admission_reject_rate < 1% for healthy pools. Gradual ramp with per-tenant overrides.

Links / Artifacts:
- Spike PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2345
- Design notes (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Slot+Quotas+and+Deferred+Eviction
- Grafana dashboard (draft): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/kv-compaction

Next steps / action items:
- [ ] Finalize slot size heuristics and per-route defaults (owner: Liam)
- [ ] Complete compactor prototype and perf run (owner: Ming Zhao)
- [ ] Add per-route fallback config UI in Console (PM: Sofia Martinez)
- [ ] Security review for NVMe-backed compressed store (Snyk scan + threat model)

Incident context (why now):
- Incident 2026-02-22 (postmortem linked in Confluence) showed two OOMs where eviction latencies > 200ms caused active batches to crash and upstream retries to cascade. This ticket encodes a deterministic, bounded-memory strategy to avoid similar outages.
